taxonomic_note: Current Kew/POWO and Flora of North America accept Rhus copallinum var. lanceolata. The familiar Texas name Rhus lanceolata is retained prominently for field continuity and for Joey/source records.
look_here_first: Start with the compound leaf: many narrow lance-shaped leaflets sit along a conspicuously winged rachis. Then confirm the deciduous, clonal shrub/small-tree habit and vivid red fall color.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays — UT PRC Purola natural flora under Rhus lanceolata; Travis — UT PRC herbarium index under the homotypic synonym; Williamson — UT PRC county treatment. Current taxonomy maps those records to R. copallinum var. lanceolata.

best_field_traits: many narrow lanceolate leaflets on an odd-pinnate leaf
rachis conspicuously winged between leaflet pairs
deciduous clonal shrub or small tree with vivid red/orange fall foliage
dense terminal panicles produce dark-red hairy flattened drupes
morphology_keys.habit: Deciduous, thicket-forming shrub or small tree.
morphology_keys.leaf_morphology: Usually about 13–21 narrow lanceolate leaflets; upper surface darker/glossier, lower surface paler to hairy.
morphology_keys.rachis: Strongly winged between leaflet pairs — one of the fastest field characters.
morphology_keys.fruit: Dark-red hairy flattened drupes in dense pyramidal clusters.
morphology_keys.joey_field_observation: Joey Santore video frame labeled Rhus lanceolata shows the compound-leaved small-tree habit; current project taxonomy reconciles that source name to Rhus copallinum var. lanceolata.

comparisons.key_distinctions: R. virens has only 5–9 thick entire evergreen leaflets and no strongly winged rachis. R. aromatica has exactly 3 leaflets. Toxicodendron should not be separated by 'leaves of three' alone; inspect habit, leaflet architecture and fruit placement/color.
